items.prompt: In this unit, what does it mean for an argument to be valid?
choices: It sounds convincing to most listeners
The reasons actually support the conclusion
The speaker sincerely believes every word they say
items.explanation: Valid is about structure: do the reasons support the conclusion. Sounding convincing or sincere is a different matter.

items.prompt: What does persuasive mean here?
choices: Every premise in it has been carefully fact-checked
Its conclusion happens to be true in the real world
It feels convincing to the listener
items.explanation: Persuasive describes the effect on a listener, which can be high even when the reasoning is poor.

items.prompt: A fallacy is best described as which of these?
choices: A recurring, nameable pattern of flawed reasoning
A statement that is simply false
Any argument that someone disagrees with
items.explanation: A fallacy is a recurring, nameable shape of reasoning that fails to support its conclusion, not just a false or unpopular claim.

items.prompt: Can a fallacious argument come from an honest speaker?
choices: No, a fallacy always signals deliberate bad faith
Yes, honesty and structure are separate
Only when the speaker is actively trying to win
items.explanation: Nobody in the game-night thread lied. The flaw was in how reasons connected to conclusions.

items.prompt: Your mind just changed after hearing a message. What has that shown?
choices: That its reasoning has been shown to be valid
That the speaker must be an expert on it
That it persuaded, not yet that it was valid
items.explanation: A changed mind shows persuasion. Whether the reasons support the claim still has to be checked.

items.prompt: In the game-night thread, what was wrong with the three messages?
choices: Their reasoning structure, not anyone's honesty
Everyone was lying about attendance
The messages were too long to read
items.explanation: The reasoning shape was flawed even though everyone believed what they typed.

items.prompt: Why name a fallacy rather than say that sounds off?
choices: A name pinpoints exactly what went wrong
Names make you sound better educated than others
Naming ends the disagreement as soon as it is said
items.explanation: A precise name tells everyone which move to correct, unlike a vague feeling.

items.prompt: Which question separates the reason from the conclusion?
choices: How many people agreed in the chat message?
What was claimed, and what reason was given?
Which person happened to type the first message?
items.explanation: Separating the claim, the reason, and the jump between them is the first step in checking any argument.

items.prompt: A friend delivers an argument with total confidence and the whole table nods along. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: That it is valid, because a whole table found it convincing
That it is invalid, because confident delivery tends to hide flaws
Only that it persuaded; validity needs a separate check
That it is valid, because this friend has often been right before
items.explanation: Agreement and confidence measure persuasion. Validity requires checking whether the stated reasons support the conclusion.
items.reference:
Two separate questions
Does it FEEL convincing? (persuasive)
Do the reasons SUPPORT the conclusion? (valid)
A fallacy: yes to the first, no to the second
Why: feeling convinced measures the listener, not the structure of the reasoning.
items.learnMore:
Persuasive is not the same as valid

Persuasiveness describes the effect on a listener. Validity describes whether the reasons given actually support the conclusion. Fallacies live in the gap between the two, and they need no dishonesty to appear.

Common mistake

Treating the fact that you changed your mind as proof the argument was sound.
items.reflection: Recall a time a confident explanation convinced you and later fell apart. What could you have asked at that moment to separate the feeling from the reasons?

items.prompt: Two arguments reach the same true conclusion. One cites evidence for it; the other says trust me, I always know. What separates them?
choices: Only the first links its reasons to its conclusion, so only it can be checked
Nothing separates them, since both of them reached the same true conclusion
The second is stronger, because confident certainty saves the table real time
The first is weaker, because evidence offered can always be disputed later
items.explanation: A true conclusion does not repair an argument that gives nothing to check. The first can be examined; the second asks for faith.

items.prompt: A speaker uses a fallacy, but their conclusion turns out to be true. What follows?
choices: The conclusion must be false because the argument was flawed
The argument becomes valid once its conclusion is confirmed
The fallacy no longer counts since nothing false was claimed
The conclusion may stand, but this argument gave no good reason to believe it
items.explanation: A flawed argument tells you nothing about the conclusion's truth either way. It only means that argument did not earn it.

items.prompt: Someone says: I felt convinced, so the reasoning must be fine. What is the mistake?
choices: Confusing a feeling with a sincere belief about the facts of the matter
Treating the effect on the listener as evidence about the reasoning's structure
Assuming the speaker must be a recognized authority on the topic at hand
Believing that persuasion only really works on listeners who are poorly informed
items.explanation: Feeling convinced is an outcome in the listener. It does not show that the reasons support the claim, so it prompts a check instead of replacing one.

items.prompt: What is a false dichotomy?
choices: Any question that has more than three answers
A disagreement that involves exactly two people
Two options presented as the only ones when others exist
items.explanation: The flaw is hiding real alternatives behind an either/or.

items.prompt: Either we commit every week or game night is over hides which option?
choices: A reminder text
Cancelling the Friday night for good
Everyone committing to every single week
items.explanation: The reminder text is a real alternative that the claim never mentions. The other two choices are the claim's own options.

items.prompt: Is the invite either went out or it did not a false dichotomy?
choices: Yes, every either/or sentence is one of them
No, those really are the only two possibilities
Yes, because invites can sometimes be sent late
items.explanation: A genuine binary is not a fallacy. The fallacy needs real alternatives to be hidden.

items.prompt: Which check exposes a false dichotomy?
choices: Count how many words each option contains
Name a real third option left out
Ask who proposed the either/or first
items.explanation: If you can point to something the claim excluded, the either/or was incomplete.

items.prompt: Which phrasing often signals a false dichotomy?
choices: Because... therefore... with a cited study attached
Some... but not all... with figures attached
Either... or... with a middle ground sitting nearby
items.explanation: An either/or framing with an unnamed middle is the usual tell.

items.prompt: A claim lists A and B, but C, D and E are also real. The list was
choices: Complete, and therefore perfectly valid
Incomplete, but presented as if it were complete
Irrelevant to the argument
items.explanation: Presenting a partial list as exhaustive is the whole fallacy.

items.prompt: For ship today or we are an unserious team, a real third option is
choices: Ship today despite lingering doubts
Admit the team is not serious
Ship tomorrow after testing
items.explanation: The other two are the claim's own options. Tomorrow morning is something neither covers.

items.prompt: Why can a false dichotomy feel natural?
choices: Two extremes are vivid and the middle goes unmentioned
Two options are statistically the most common ones
Listeners dislike considering more than one idea at once
items.explanation: Extremes are vivid, and silence about the middle makes it feel absent rather than hidden.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a genuine either/or rather than a false dichotomy?
choices: This ordinary light switch is either on or off right now
You are either with this plan or against the whole team
Either we cut the budget entirely or this whole project simply dies
Either you love the game or you should stay home
items.explanation: Only the switch has exactly two states. The others hide options such as partial support, scope cuts, or occasional play.
items.reference:
The possibility-space check
Claimed: commit weekly / admit it is over
Hidden: reminder text, rotate hosts, accept an occasional miss
Any real hidden option makes the either/or false
Why: the fallacy is presenting an incomplete list of options as if it were complete.
items.learnMore:
Naming the missing third option

To test an either/or claim, list what is genuinely possible and compare it with what was offered. If you can name one real option the claim silently excluded, the dichotomy was false. If the space really has two members, it was not a fallacy at all.

Common mistake

Calling every either/or sentence a false dichotomy, including ones that are truly binary.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you were once told came down to two choices. What third option existed that nobody said out loud?

items.prompt: Someone says: either we skip the dinner or we all cancel our weekend plans. Which reply best shows the dichotomy is false?
choices: Say that cancelling every weekend plan is a bad idea
Say that the speaker is being dramatic about all this
Ask how many people at the table want to skip the dinner
Show that a shorter dinner on Saturday fits both
items.explanation: A concrete third option that satisfies both sides is the direct test. The other replies argue about the options or the speaker instead.

items.prompt: Someone offers three options, A, B or C, and says nothing else exists. Can the same error occur?
choices: Yes, since the flaw is hiding real options, whatever the count
No, the fallacy needs exactly two options
No, three options always cover everything
Yes, but only when C is the speaker's favorite
items.explanation: The count is not the point. Any exhaustive-sounding list that omits real options has the same flaw.

items.prompt: Last Friday 2 of 6 friends missed (a 33% miss rate). A reminder text would cut misses by 40%. About how many attend on average?
choices: About 4.0 of 6
About 4.8 of 6
About 5.6 of 6
About 3.2 of 6
items.explanation: Misses drop from 33% to 20%, so about 1.2 of 6 miss and 4.8 attend. This is why the excluded reminder text is a real option, not a dodge.

items.prompt: What is a straw man?
choices: Rebutting a distorted version of the claim
Attacking the speaker's character and past record
Citing an expert who works in a different field
items.explanation: The arguer attacks a version of the claim that is easier to beat than the real one.

items.prompt: What is an ad hominem?
choices: Exaggerating the claim, then rebutting it
Attacking the person making the claim instead of the claim
Offering only two options
items.explanation: The claim itself is never engaged. The person making it is the target.

items.prompt: So you want us to guilt-trip anyone who is busy? replying to try a reminder text is a
choices: Straw man
Ad hominem
Slippery slope
items.explanation: Nobody proposed guilt-tripping. The reply swapped in a more extreme position.

items.prompt: Jamie only says that because Jamie picks the games is a
choices: Straw man
Ad hominem
False dichotomy
items.explanation: It targets Jamie's motive and never asks whether Jamie's point is right.

items.prompt: The best first fix for a straw man is to
choices: Attack their wording right back
Drop the topic
Restate your real claim precisely, so the group can answer it
items.explanation: Naming what you actually said gives the group something real to respond to.

items.prompt: Can an ad hominem remark be true?
choices: Yes, but it still does not address the claim
No, since then it would count as relevant evidence
No, true statements are never fallacies
items.explanation: Truth about a person does not show their claim is wrong.

items.prompt: A straw man replaces your claim with
choices: A stronger version backed up by data
A weaker or more extreme version
An identical claim worded differently
items.explanation: The swapped-in version is chosen because it is easier to knock down.

items.prompt: What does an ad hominem skip?
choices: Whether the speaker was being polite
Whether the topic is interesting
Whether the claim itself is correct
items.explanation: The claim's merits never get examined.

items.prompt: Reply to we should try a reminder text: you just want to avoid the effort of hosting. Which fallacy is this?
choices: Ad hominem, since it targets a supposed motive instead of the proposal
Straw man, since it distorts the proposal into something far more extreme
False dichotomy, since it offers only two readings of the proposal
Slippery slope, since it predicts a long chain of consequences
items.explanation: The reply never evaluates the reminder idea. It speculates about the person's reasons for suggesting it.
items.reference:
Two ways to dodge the real claim
Straw man: swap in a weaker or more extreme claim
Ad hominem: swap the claim for the person
Fix: restate the real claim, then answer it
Why: both replace what was said with something easier to attack.
items.learnMore:
Restating the real claim

When someone distorts your position, naming the fallacy is only half the job. The correction is to say precisely what you did claim, so the group can answer that instead of the distortion.

Common mistake

Shouting straw man without saying what the actual position was.
items.reflection: Recall a disagreement where someone answered a position you never held. How did you feel, and what could you have said first?

items.prompt: Someone says maybe we should check the schedule first. A reply: so you think we should never make spontaneous plans? What is the best correction?
choices: That is a personal attack, and it is not fair to say
I did not say never; I said check this one plan
You are wrong about spontaneous plans in general as well
Everyone here already agrees with me on this point
items.explanation: A good correction restates the real claim. The other replies argue about fairness, add a new dispute, or lean on the crowd.

items.prompt: Is mentioning that a speaker sells the product they recommend always an ad hominem?
choices: Yes, any mention of a speaker's interests attacks the person
No, because interests never affect whether a claim is true
Yes, unless the speaker admits the interest first
No, it can be relevant context, provided the claim is still evaluated on its merits
items.explanation: Context about who benefits can prompt closer scrutiny. It becomes a fallacy only when it replaces looking at the claim.

items.prompt: A reply restates the other side's claim accurately, then argues against it. Which statement is right?
choices: That is a straw man because it is a rebuttal
That is not a straw man, however sharp the rebuttal is
That depends entirely on whether the rebuttal ends up winning
That is an ad hominem because it opposes a particular person
items.explanation: A straw man needs a distortion. Disagreeing with an accurately stated claim is just ordinary argument.

items.prompt: A slippery slope claims that
choices: Only two options exist
A person's motive discredits their claim
A small step inevitably cascades into an extreme outcome
items.explanation: The fallacy is asserting the cascade without showing how it happens.

items.prompt: What is missing in a slippery slope?
choices: A mechanism linking each step to the next
A famous and widely respected source to cite
A second possible option to compare it against
items.explanation: Without a mechanism, the chain of dominoes is only asserted.

items.prompt: When is an appeal to authority misused?
choices: Whenever any expert is mentioned at all
Whenever the expert named is very famous indeed
When the expertise is about a different question
items.explanation: Authority counts for what it actually covers, and no further.

items.prompt: A therapist uncle says friend groups always collapse. What is borrowed?
choices: A statistic from a study
Real expertise applied to a claim it does not settle
A direct observation
items.explanation: General expertise on groups does not decide whether this group, after one dip, is declining.

items.prompt: Is citing a doctor's view on a medical question a fallacy?
choices: No, relevant expertise is rightly weighed
Yes, every appeal to authority is a fallacy
Yes, since doctors are sometimes wrong too
items.explanation: The fallacy is the misuse, not the appeal. Relevant expertise deserves weight.

items.prompt: If we let two people skip, game night will die is a
choices: Slippery slope
Ad hominem
Appeal to authority
items.explanation: A small bounded event is claimed to end in a collapse without a mechanism.

items.prompt: Which quick test checks an appeal to authority?
choices: Is the expertise about this exact question?
Is the authority widely known by name?
Does the authority agree with what I already think?
items.explanation: Fame and agreement are irrelevant. Coverage of the specific question is what matters.

items.prompt: A legitimate cascade argument would include
choices: A louder description of the final outcome
A longer list of other possible outcomes
A reason each step leads to the next
items.explanation: Mechanisms, not volume or length, make a chain of consequences credible.

items.prompt: Which is a legitimate use of authority rather than a misused one?
choices: A structural engineer's view on whether this beam can carry the load
A celebrated architect's view on whether the company should merge
A famous chef's view on whether this bridge is actually safe
A bestselling author's view on how this particular beam will hold up
items.explanation: Only the engineer's expertise covers the exact question asked. The others borrow prestige from a different field.
items.reference:
Two tests
Authority: is the expertise about THIS exact question?
Slope: is there a mechanism from each step to the next?
No to either: the argument borrows weight it has not earned
Why: credentials and dramatic endpoints are not substitutes for reasons.
items.learnMore:
Borrowed weight

A misused authority lends real credibility from one question to a different one. A slippery slope lends the drama of an extreme outcome to a modest first step. In both, the reasons that should connect premise to conclusion are missing.

Common mistake

Dismissing all appeals to expertise, even relevant ones, or all cascade arguments, even well-supported ones.
items.reflection: Think of a claim you accepted because of who said it. Would the same person be an expert on that exact question?

items.prompt: Skip one practice and soon you will skip them all and quit. What would turn this into a reasoned claim?
choices: Evidence of how one skip actually leads to the next
Repeating the same claim again with far more confidence
Adding a second dramatic outcome to the end of the chain
Quoting a well known coach who happens to agree with it
items.explanation: A mechanism for each step is what the slope lacked. Confidence, extra drama, and a quote do not supply one.

items.prompt: Every step in a chain is shown to cause the next. Is it still a slippery slope fallacy?
choices: Yes, any chain of consequences is a fallacy
No, since the fallacy is the missing mechanism, not the cascade itself
Yes, if the final outcome is extreme enough
No, but only when the steps are small ones
items.explanation: Real cascades exist. The error is claiming one without showing the links.

items.prompt: An expert says in my field this is settled, but the claim is about a nearby field. What is the best reaction?
choices: Accept it right away, since genuine experts rarely turn out to be wrong
Dismiss everything this expert says as worthless from here on in
Ask whether their expertise covers this exact question before weighing it
Treat the comment as an ad hominem attack against the expert, so ignore it
items.explanation: Their knowledge may be real but only partly relevant. Check the coverage instead of accepting or rejecting wholesale.

items.prompt: What makes naming a fallacy useful?
choices: It signals clearly that the other person has lost
It saves the effort of reading the whole thread
A precise label plus a restated real claim
items.explanation: The label pinpoints the move and the restated claim gets the thread back on track.

items.prompt: After naming a straw man, the group still needs to
choices: Find out who started it
Answer the original question they began with
End the thread quickly
items.explanation: Clearing away a distortion only restores the path to the real question.

items.prompt: Is every either/or sentence a fallacy?
choices: No, some are genuinely binary
Yes, every one of them is a fallacy
Only when posted in a group chat
items.explanation: Over-applying the label erodes its meaning.

items.prompt: Does calling out a fallacy win the disagreement?
choices: Yes, because the other side must then concede
Yes, provided you were the one who named it first
No, it only clears the path to the real question
items.explanation: The underlying judgment still has to be made.

items.prompt: Multiple fallacies in one thread
choices: Can occur together, with one provoking another
Never appear in the same thread
Cancel each other out
items.explanation: A false dichotomy provoked a straw man in the game-night thread. Each move needs its own response.

items.prompt: A useful callout template includes
choices: A ranked verdict on who argued worst in the thread
The name, your real claim, and the open question
A list of every fallacy ever named, in order
items.explanation: Those three parts name the move, correct it, and refocus the thread.

items.prompt: Seeing fallacies everywhere is
choices: A sign of especially strong and careful reasoning
Harmless, since fallacy labels cost nothing to use
A failure mode that weakens the labels
items.explanation: Crying wolf makes real fallacies easier to dismiss.

items.prompt: How did the fallacy-free game-night thread end?
choices: Game night being cancelled for good
Reminders tried, attendance checked in four weeks
The group deciding it was doomed anyway after all
items.explanation: The clean version still made a real judgment call: test a low-cost fix and look at the numbers.

items.prompt: Which reply uses a fallacy name well?
choices: Straw man: I proposed a reminder text, not guilt-tripping. Does attendance show a real trend?
Straw man! You are arguing against something I never said, so this whole thread is meaningless now
That is a fallacy, so everything you said before it is invalid and we can stop discussing it here
Stop using fallacies and just answer the question the way I asked it in the first place today
items.explanation: A good callout names the move, restates the real claim, and returns to the open question. The others only declare victory.
items.reference:
A useful callout has three parts
1. The pattern name
2. Your version of the real claim
3. The question still to answer
Why: naming a fallacy clears a path; it does not make the judgment call for you.
items.learnMore:
Names are a tool, not a verdict

Used well, a fallacy name plus a restated claim moves a thread back to the real question. Used as a weapon, it is just another way to avoid that question. A fallacy-free thread still has to answer it.

Common mistake

Treating I named the fallacy as the end of the conversation.
items.reflection: Think of a recent disagreement. Which part of it was the real question, and what moves pulled the conversation away from it?

items.prompt: A thread shows a false dichotomy answered by a straw man. How should you respond?
choices: Give one blanket objection that the whole thread is full of fallacies
Ignore the first move entirely and answer only the last message in the thread
Answer each move separately, restating the real claim for the second
Ask both people to apologize and then restart the whole thread afresh
